content: Health educators, physical education teachers, office staff, and parent-teacher groups should be actively involved in asthma management programs within schools. Focus groups consisting of school staff can provide detailed insights to develop effective interventions. Schools should aim to implement strategies that support the entire school community in managing asthma. It is essential to involve all school staff, parents, and students in these efforts. To address asthma and other student health issues comprehensively, schools should establish a health committee or utilize an existing one to address asthma-related needs. Children with asthma require adequate support at school to manage their condition effectively and participate fully in activities. The handbook titled How Asthma Friendly is Your School? serves as a valuable resource for assessing how well a school accommodates children with asthma. This handbook includes a seven-item checklist in a scorecard format, which parents, teachers, and school nurses can use to identify specific areas that may pose challenges for children with asthma. It also helps these stakeholders gain support from school administrators to implement asthma-friendly policies and practices. Examples of policies schools can adopt include ensuring quick and reliable access to medications, requiring individualized asthma management plans from physicians, preparing for asthma emergencies, providing preand after-school care for children with asthma, and promoting safe and inclusive participation in all school activities. Child-care facilities are another critical area for asthma interventions. The Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America (AAFA) has developed an educational package called Asthma and Allergy Essentials for Child Care Providers. This program educates providers on recognizing asthma and allergy symptoms, implementing environmental control measures to prevent episodes, and properly using medications and equipment for asthma management. An environmental checklist is included to identify allergens and irritants that may affect a child’s breathing. This program is available in areas served by AAFA chapters. Professional education is vital for clinicians who diagnose and treat asthma. Effective asthma management requires ongoing collaboration among patients, caregivers, and healthcare providers. Providers must stay updated on new medical therapies and self-management approaches. Additionally, healthcare providers face challenges related to healthcare delivery and business issues, necessitating collaborative education that addresses the full scope of asthma case management. Physicians are often most receptive to information from respected peers, particularly opinion leaders in the field. Time constraints are a significant barrier to education for healthcare professionals, so strategies like problem-based learning and hands-on application of new skills are effective, though resource-intensive. Educational efforts should focus on changing provider behaviors rather than merely presenting information. Providers should be guided on key behaviors and messages to use during routine asthma care, emphasizing that quality and efficiency can improve with these changes. Asthma care involves various healthcare providers, including physicians, nurses, clinical staff, emergency department personnel, and pharmacy staff. Consistent education should be provided to all members of the asthma management team. Occupational asthma is another area of concern. Surveillance projects, such as the NIOSH Occupational Asthma Identification Project, collect data on respiratory symptoms and diseases among at-risk workers. Primary-care providers should be educated about the role of workplace exposures in causing or exacerbating asthma, enabling them to help patients identify triggers and refer them to specialists. Work-related asthma should also be integrated into broader asthma surveillance and intervention activities. Environmental interventions are a crucial component of state asthma programs. Education and outreach strategies should inform audiences about environmental factors that exacerbate asthma and ways to reduce or eliminate exposures. Examples include public service messages about asthma triggers, air-quality advisory networks, and outreach to physicians about assessing residential or workplace exposures. Educational efforts should target individual patients, families, healthcare providers, community organizations, government agencies, landlords, employers, workers, and schools, with tailored messages for each audience. It is important to note that allergens only cause reactions in individuals with specific allergies.
